newsitem.title: THAILAND: Exporters urge Thai government to beat hurdles.
newsitem.headline: Exporters urge Thai government to beat hurdles.

text.p: Thai exporters on Sunday urged the government to quickly overcome obstacles hindering their export competitiveness if an official 1997 export growth target of 10 percent was to be achieved.
The modest 10 percent export growth target for next year follows government expectations for dismal zero percent growth this year after 23.6 percent in 1995.

"The 10 percent export growth next year is feasible (but) to achieve this, the government must support and seriously solve several major obstacles undermining our export competitiveness," Surapon Vongvattanaroje, president of Surapon Seafoods Plc, told Reuters.
Surapon was one of a large group of businessmen attending a commerce ministry seminar on strategies to boost Thailand's exports and cut imports for 1997.
In its latest report at the seminar on Friday, the ministry said Thailand's 1997 exports were projected to grow by 10 percent to 1.58 trillion baht ($63.12 billion).

"Our export (growth) in 1997 will not be as bad as this year. The expected export growth of 10 percent next year is the minimum target," Commerce Minister Narongchai Akrasanee told the seminar's closing session.

Other exporters at the seminar said a delay in value-added tax (VAT) refunds by the government to exporters and high tariffs on raw materials for production were among the key hurdles in promoting exports.

Vilai Kiatsrichart, president of the Thai Canned Food Association said: "Every involved party already knows what the problems are that obstruct our exports. All it needs is quick actions from the government to overcome them."

Narongchai said the government would try to resolve these problems. He said because of the remedial measures that would be taken, export growth in 1997 would likely rise to 15 percent against the ministry's earlier projection of 10 percent.
Imports, on the other hand, would be lower than the official target as government policy would be tightened to curb public and private spending on imported goods, he said.

Thailand suffers from a severe current account deficit, one of the highest in the region. The government forecast this year's deficit would rise to 8.3 percent of gross domestic product from 8.1 percent in 1995.
The commerce ministry has projected imports would grow by 14.97 percent to 2.17 trillion baht in 1997, compared with projected imports of 1.89 trillion this year.
The trade deficit was also expected to rise sharply to 595 billion baht, compared with 455 billion seen for this year, the ministry said.
